name: Example Specificity Score
description: Scores specificity and verifiability of examples — AI-generated examples tend to be generic, vague, or fabricated.
mechanism:
This method applies Example Specificity Score for AI-generated content detection:

1. **Example Span Detection**: The method identifies example spans in text using discourse cue detection — phrases like "for example", "for instance", "such as", "e.g.", "consider the case of", "take X", "as illustrated by", and unmarked examples introduced by colons or dashes. Additionally, the method detects implicit examples: concrete instances embedded in argumentation without explicit markers. Detection uses a combination of cue phrase matching and semantic role labeling to identify illustrative content. Human text uses 4–8 examples per 1000 words; AI text uses 3–6 per 1000 words. The key difference is not frequency but specificity — human examples are concrete and verifiable; AI examples are generic and interchangeable.

2. **Specificity Dimension Scoring**: Each detected example is scored on four specificity dimensions (0–1 scale): (a) Named entities — does the example reference specific people, places, organizations, dates? Score based on NER density within the example span. A specific example ("When Toyota implemented lean manufacturing in their Georgetown, Kentucky plant in 1988...") scores 0.9; a generic one ("When companies implement new processes...") scores 0.1. (b) Quantitative detail — does the example include specific numbers, measurements, or statistics? (c) Experiential texture — does the example include sensory, emotional, or situational details that suggest firsthand knowledge? Measured via concreteness ratings from the Brysbaert et al. (2014) norms. (d) Causal specificity — does the example explain why/how something happened, or just that it happened? Human examples average composite specificity of 0.55–0.75; AI examples average 0.20–0.40.

3. **Example-Argument Fit Analysis**: The method evaluates how well each example supports its surrounding argument using semantic similarity and entailment. Good examples are: (a) relevant — semantically connected to the claim (cosine similarity > 0.6 between example and claim embeddings), (b) illustrative — demonstrating the claim rather than restating it (entailment without paraphrase), (c) appropriately scoped — matching the generality of the claim (specific examples for specific claims). AI examples frequently suffer from scope mismatch: generic examples supporting specific claims, or examples that restate the claim rather than illustrating it. Fit scores: human 0.65–0.80; AI 0.40–0.55.

4. **Example Recycling and Template Detection**: AI text tends to generate examples from a limited inventory of patterns. The method detects: (a) template examples — following recognizable patterns like "Company X did Y and saw Z% improvement", where specific values are slotted into a template. (b) Interchangeability — whether the example could apply to any similar claim without modification. The method tests this by computing semantic distance between the example and a randomly selected claim from the same domain. Highly interchangeable examples (distance < 0.3) suggest AI generation. (c) Example diversity — across a text, human writers use varied example types (personal anecdotes, historical cases, data, thought experiments); AI concentrates on 1–2 types. Type diversity entropy: human 1.6–2.2 bits; AI 0.6–1.2 bits.
parameters:
Example detection cues: 12+ discourse markers + implicit patterns
Specificity dimensions: 4 (named entities, quantitative, experiential, causal)
Human specificity: 0.55–0.75
AI specificity: 0.20–0.40
Example-argument fit human: 0.65–0.80
Example-argument fit AI: 0.40–0.55
Interchangeability threshold: < 0.3 (AI-like)
Type diversity human: 1.6–2.2 bits
Type diversity AI: 0.6–1.2 bits
Minimum examples for analysis: 3
accuracy: 78–87% accuracy detecting AI-generated text via example specificity analysis. Composite specificity scoring achieves AUC of 0.84. Template detection adds 4–5% improvement. Example-argument fit provides F1-score of 0.81. Performance best for argumentative, explanatory, and educational text.
source: Brysbaert, M. et al. (2014). Concreteness ratings for 40 thousand generally known English word lemmas. Behavior Research Methods, 46(3), 904–911.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated essays and articles through generic example patterns. Evaluating writing quality in educational assessment. Identifying AI-written content marketing through template examples. Assessing evidence quality in student papers.
strengths:
• Targets a specific weakness of AI — inability to produce verifiable concrete examples
• Named entity density is a strong standalone discriminator
• Example-argument fit captures rhetorical competence
• Template detection catches systematic AI patterns
• Complements evidence quality and factual density methods
limitations:
• Some genres (philosophy, abstract theory) legitimately use generic examples
• Short texts may contain too few examples for analysis
• Human writers in unfamiliar domains may also produce vague examples
• Fictional and hypothetical examples are intentionally non-verifiable
• AI fine-tuned on specific domains may produce more specific examples
